title: Apple changes full-disk access permissions to curb abuse from AI agents
gist: Apple is tightening macOS Full Disk Access after Meta's Muse AI agent reportedly surfaced a user's private Messages thread despite Meta saying access required opt-in. Combined with a Muse hijack flaw and Amazon blocking the agent, the episode shows OS-level permissions are becoming the control point for autonomous AI assistants.

themes.theme: Apple tightens Full Disk Access for AI agents

insights.claim: Apple says it is changing macOS privacy settings to stop third-party developers from misusing Full Disk Access to reach message histories, and warns that risk rises as AI agents become more capable and autonomous.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Platform owners are positioning as gatekeepers of agent access, which shapes which agent products can function on Apple devices.
insights.quote: As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially.

insights.claim: Apple argues that for communication apps, over-broad disk access also compromises the privacy of the other people a user communicates with, not just the user.
insights.speaker: Apple
insights.so_what: Third-party privacy exposure raises regulatory and liability risk for agent makers who ingest messages.
insights.quote: For communication apps, this can also compromise the privacy of the people users are communicating with.
insights.locator: Some developers are using Full Disk Access

insights.claim: Apple did not name Meta or Muse, but the timing after a social media uproar makes it likely the change responds to the Muse incident, and Apple's statements seem to contradict Meta's denial.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Signals friction between platform owners and AI-agent entrants, a competitive dynamic worth tracking for Meta and Apple.

insights.claim: Columnist Jason Aten said Meta's Muse agent sent him an unsolicited notification referencing a private thread with a co-worker in Apple Messages, though he says he never granted it message permissions.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A reputational risk event for Meta's agent launch that could slow consumer trust and adoption.
insights.locator: Friday's announcement comes two weeks after

insights.claim: Meta CTO David Singleton says Muse can read Messages only if both macOS Full Disk Access and the Muse Messages connector are enabled, implying the user was responsible.
insights.speaker: David Singleton
insights.so_what: Meta's defence relies on user consent design, which is now being challenged by the platform owner.
insights.quote: Your Muse can only read Messages content if macOS system-level Full Disk Access is granted and the Messages connector is enabled.

insights.claim: Security expert Patrick Wardle disputes Singleton's denial, arguing that any app with Full Disk Access can read any non-root file, including chats and browser data.
insights.speaker: Patrick Wardle
insights.so_what: Full Disk Access is an all-or-nothing grant, so connector toggles offer weak protection in practice.
insights.quote: From a technical point of view, with FDA (full-disk access), any (non-root file), is readable, browsing history, browser cookies, chats, etc etc etc.
insights.locator: Earlier this week, I spoke to macOS security expert

insights.claim: Meta PR only repeated Singleton's quote when asked how Muse could not read messages while other Full Disk Access apps could, and did not answer further questions.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: An unresolved communications posture suggests lingering reputational overhang for Meta.

insights.claim: Eleven days before Apple's announcement, Wardle disclosed a Muse configuration that let any app or code on a Mac, including commands injected via ClickFix attacks, take full control of the assistant and its resources.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: An agent with broad access is a high-value attack surface, so agent security tooling is a likely growth area.

insights.claim: Amazon blocked Muse from its platform, saying such apps should operate openly and respect service providers' decisions about participating.
insights.speaker: Amazon
insights.so_what: Large platforms are walling off their services from third-party agents, limiting agent utility and reinforcing walled gardens.
insights.quote: should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate
insights.locator: It also comes after Amazon blocked Muse

insights.claim: Social media reaction framed AI assistants with access to calendars, email, messages and shopping accounts as akin to power tools that are useful but can do real damage if used carelessly.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Consumer trust in permissioned agents is fragile and one incident can shift sentiment.
insights.locator: Social media last week blew up

insights.claim: The author concludes Muse may not be worthy of the extraordinary access it needs to work as Meta advertises, and notes that careful permission configuration only goes so far.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Skepticism toward Meta's agent suggests slower adoption for products requiring deep device access.
insights.quote: Muse may not be worthy of the extraordinary access it must have to work as billed by Meta.
